item.title: Attention Is Only as Good as Its Witnesses: When Higher-Order Layers Help, and When They Do Not
item.dc:creator: Mostafa 'Neo' Mohsenvand
item.description:
Theorems on the depth-law construction, the size law, and the character-based SET pair counting are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib and released with the code.
Transformers stop learning graph search as graphs grow, and learn the card game SET only after many distinct questions, although attention can represent both. We read these failures, and the uneven record of higher-order attention, from what a layer sums over: each layer we study computes the partition function of a family of witnesses and reads it at a temperature. Two laws follow. The depth law is a known result of logic, which we state for these layers: L layers over two-step walks reach exactly 2^L - 1 steps, just as a logical statement with L nested clauses of the form "there is a vertex such that" sees exactly that far. We build a construction that reaches this far, checked in Lean, and, when vertices carry no names, no such network reaches further. The size law is the cost of reading at a temperature, which logic does not have: existence is read correctly at every size, in the worst case, if and only if inverse temperature times margin is at least the logarithm of the number of candidates. Layers built on these laws, and on two principles that we test, learn where Transformers fail. One propagator layer trained on 49-vertex graphs answers every question at every search depth on 250-vertex graphs. Given the modulus 3, exponential Newton computes the softmax of 2-simplicial attention over pairs exactly in 3^d n operations for d clocks; with six clocks it learns SET from as few deals as 2-simplicial attention and transfers from 8- to 20-card tables. On CLRS-30 without hints, a 186,000-parameter block of OR-join and power-mean channels matches (within half a point) or beats a model of at least 73 million parameters on 9 of 12 graph tasks of the official test set, and on 8 of 12 with freshly drawn test graphs. The same account explains where pair layers did not help and where parallel layers must loop.

item.title: An iterated-logarithm price of anytime validity for log-optimal e-processes
item.dc:creator: Adrien Corenflos
item.description:
All lemmas, propositions, and theorems on minimax regret of e-processes are formalized in Lean with Mathlib, aided by Claude; formalization exposed a gap.
Log-optimal e-variables at fixed horizons, also called numéraires, have been conjectured to “almost” form an e-process for exponential-family null hypotheses. A related open question is whether an e-process can attain the optimal e-power at every horizon up to a bounded loss. Given a final horizon, we study the minimax regret of e-processes relative to the numéraires at all times up to it. For the Gaussian location null and the composite alternative of Gaussian distributions with a smaller variance and an unknown location, we show that the minimax regret in the worst case over the location grows like the iterated logarithm of the final horizon. A single e-process attains this rate at every horizon. This growth answers the question negatively. It also refutes the conjecture if “almost” means a regret bounded uniformly over horizons. For this Gaussian location problem, we thus exhibit the frontier precisely: the minimax regret is bounded if and only if the alternatives have at least the variance of the null.

item.title: Operator Learning of Microstructure-Dependent Internal-Variable Models for Inelastic Homogenization: Approximation and Complexity
item.dc:creator: Lianghao Cao, George Stepaniants, Andrew M. Stuart
item.description:
The universal approximation and internal-variable complexity theorems were formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, AI-assisted, and checked against separately specified statements with Lean Comparator.
We study the learning of homogenized constitutive laws for inelastic heterogeneous materials, aiming to replace costly concurrent unit-cell simulations with surrogates that generalize across loading histories and microstructures. We focus on the recurrent neural operator framework, motivated by the explicit form of homogenized Kelvin–Voigt linear viscoelasticity. In this framework, internal variables enable a Markovian approximation of loading-history dependence, and neural operators represent the microstructure-dependent constitutive response. For periodic Kelvin–Voigt viscoelasticity, we prove a universal approximation theorem showing that the model can approximate the homogenized constitutive law to any prescribed accuracy, uniformly in time and over a wide set of admissible strain trajectories and microstructural property fields, in two and three dimensions. This comprises a significant extension of the existing, somewhat limited, one-dimensional theory that uses explicit solutions for piecewise constant materials. Instead, in two and three dimensions, we adopt a more versatile approximation based on the spectral representation of the memory kernel that arises from homogenization. This also enables us to give an explicit bound on the internal-variable dimension, sufficient for approximation, exhibiting logarithmic growth in the inverse relative stress error and in material contrast. Numerical experiments on viscoelasticity and crystal plasticity complement the theory, illustrating the roles of internal-variable dimension and sample complexity in learning homogenized responses from unit-cell data. Theoretical results are formally verified in Lean 4.

item.title: Binary Belief Propagation Fixed Points: Finiteness, Rigidity, and Topological Complexity
item.dc:creator: Yusuke Watanabe
item.description:
The three main theorems on belief propagation fixed points, including the logarithmic size bounds, are formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib and the Tau Ceti differential topology library.
A fixed finite binary Ising model has only finitely many admissible complex belief propagation fixed points, even at degenerate parameter values. Families of positive fixed points obtained by varying external fields can nevertheless have nontrivial topology. We study this distinction through the external-field projection. For a fixed field, we prove finiteness by bounding the pole orders of the magnetizations on a hypothetical complex solution curve. The generic degree on the support graph then bounds the total local multiplicity. A graph has a single smooth real line as its full positive response for every choice of positive couplings, base field, and strictly positive sweep direction exactly when it contains no two vertex-disjoint connected subgraphs of cycle rank at least two. Two such subgraphs suffice to create a circular component. For a plane obtained by varying two vertex fields, connected simple bipartite cubic graphs with one uniform coupling and a universal bound on the fixed fields realize every genus. The minimum number of vertices grows logarithmically in the genus, by a matching algebraic upper bound on Betti numbers. Finally, we certify the complete field discriminant of an eighteen-vertex product model and recover its torus component's genus from the counts of distinct roots on all field cells. The three main theorems, including the logarithmic size bounds, are formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib.

item.title: Spectral Stability, Fatou Basin Contraction, and Machine-Checked Multipliers in Holomorphic Extensions of Generalized Syracuse Dynamics
item.dc:creator: Volkan Dağlı, Zerrin Dağlı, Dağhan Dağlı, Emrah Yurtseven, Murat Emre Özkaya
item.description:
Twenty theorems on the Syracuse and Collatz interpolations, multipliers, Koenigs coefficients and block contraction are formalized in a Lean 4 ancillary file, with no sorry.
We embed the Syracuse operator $T(n) = n/2$ (even $n$), $T(n) = (3n+1)/2$ (odd $n$) and the Collatz map $C(n)$ into $\mathbb{C}$ via entire functions of exponential type $π$: $f(z) = \frac{1}{4}(1 + 4z - (1 + 2z)\cos(πz))$ and $F(z) = \frac{1}{4}(2 + 7z - (2 + 5z)\cos(πz))$. We prove five results: (1) every integer periodic cycle $C \subset \mathbb{N}^+$ of $T$ is a strictly attracting Fatou cycle of $f$ with multiplier $μ_f(C) = 3^{N_{\mathrm{odd}}}/2^N = \prod_{n \in C\text{ odd}} \frac{3n}{3n+1} \in (0,1)$, and $μ_f(O_{1,2}) = μ_F(O_{1,4,2}) = 3/4 < 1$; (2) on the Fatou basin $B(O_{1,2})$, $g = f^{\circ 2}$ conjugates to $Φ_j(g(z)) = \frac{3}{4}Φ_j(z)$ with Koenigs Taylor jets $c_2(1) = -\frac{13}{2}π^2$ and $d_2(2) = -\frac{9}{2}π^2$; (3) the Schwarzian derivative is strictly negative on $\mathbb{Z}$ ($S(f)(n) \le 3π^2 - \frac{3}{8}π^4 \approx -6.9196 < 0$), and a repelling Julia 2-cycle $O_{\mathrm{rep}} \subset J(f)$ ($μ\approx 1.2148 > 1$) isolates $B(O_{1,2})$; (4) on $(\mathbb{Z}_2, μ_{\mathrm{Haar}})$, the 2-adic Lyapunov exponent $λ_{\mathrm{Haar}} = \frac{1}{2}\ln(3/4) \approx -0.143841 < 0$ equals $\frac{1}{2}\ln|μ_f(O_{1,2})|$; and (5) we certify 20 theorems in Lean 4 (anc/CollatzAttractor.lean, 0 sorry). These results establish local Fatou invariants and 2-adic ergodic averages for $f(z)$, leaving open whether every $n_0 \in \mathbb{N}^+$ lies in $\bigcup_{k \ge 0} f^{-k}(B(O_{1,2}))$.

item.title: No regular icosahedron has a rational point on every face: a proof checked in Lean
item.dc:creator: Mikhail Levit
item.description:
Full proof, including 48 kernel-checked exact-arithmetic certificates over Z[φ], is formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib; formalization developed by AI under author direction.
We prove that no regular icosahedron in $\mathbb{R}^3$ has a point with rational coordinates on each of its twenty closed faces, in every position, size and orientation, reflections included. This answers a question of I. Bogdanov on MathOverflow. A field automorphism of $\mathbb{C}$ that sends $\sqrt5$ to $-\sqrt5$ reduces the problem to the following statement: for every complex orthogonal $3\times3$ matrix $T$ some real linear combination of $\mathrm{Re}\,T$ and $\mathrm{Im}\,T$ separates ten intervals determined by the faces. We prove this statement by a computer-assisted case analysis over rational parametrizations of rotation frames, in which every inequality is an exact polynomial bound over $\mathbb{Z}[\varphi]$, $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$; no floating-point arithmetic and no Lipschitz estimates are used. The whole argument, including the $48$ certificates, is formalized in the Lean 4 proof assistant with Mathlib and checked by the Lean kernel; the main theorem depends only on the standard axioms. The mathematical argument and the formalization were produced by AI systems (OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude) under the direction of the author; see the statement at the end of the paper.

item.title: Inhomogeneous deformations of $\mathfrak{osp}(N|2n)$: triviality for any number of odd parameters
item.dc:creator: Hisashi Aoi
item.description:
The main results on odd deformations of osp(N|2n) are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, defining the algebras by generators and relations, with a public GitHub artifact.
We treat a symmetrized mixed-oscillator deformation family of the orthosymplectic Lie superalgebras $\mathfrak{osp}(N|2n)$, $N,n\geq1$, with even mixed coefficients $β_{u,i}$ and one odd square-zero parameter. We derive the deformed bracket from an oscillator realization, show that its coefficient is determined by the realization, and exhibit an explicit odd primitive, normalized by its vanishing on $\mathfrak{sp}(2n)$. Every odd primitive differs from it by a unique inner derivation. For $N=1$ this is the case $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2n)$ treated earlier. With multiple odd parameters the deformed bracket is the sum of the single-parameter deformations and is again trivial. The trivialization, however, is not additive: it is the product of the single-parameter trivializations followed by a nonsymplectic change of the bosonic generators. The main results are formalized in Lean 4, with the algebras constructed by generators and relations; what is not formalized is stated in the appendix.

item.title: Keel: A Verified In-Kernel Proof Checker for Proof Carrying BPF
item.dc:creator: Yalu Cai, Tung-Che Chang, Santosh Nagarakatte
item.description:
Specifies and proves sound an eBPF proof-certificate checker in Lean 4, with a deeply embedded C fragment (EmbC) proven to refine it.
Recent systems such as the eBPF Certificate Framework (BCF) and Proof-Carrying BPF address the imprecision in the Linux eBPF verifier with proof-carrying code. When the verifier's abstract domains cannot prove a safety condition, an in-kernel proof checker checks an untrusted user-space refutation proof. A single bug in this checker can compromise the security of the entire kernel. While formalizing BCF's in-kernel checker, we discovered 13 bugs such as unsound rewrite rules, silently unchecked proof steps, and memory safety errors. We demonstrate that forged certificates can trick the kernel to accept arbitrary unsafe eBPF programs. To address this problem, we propose Keel, a formally verified in-kernel proof checker for the Linux eBPF verifier. First, we specify the checker as a pure functional program in Lean and prove its soundness against bit-vector semantics. We decouple the steps of the proof certificate checker from the mathematical rewrite rules, which enables us to extend the rewrite rules without the need to change the checker. Second, we implement the checker in EmbC, a deeply embedded C fragment, and prove that our C implementation refines the functional specification without undefined behavior or memory leaks. Third, using an amortized potential argument, we prove linear time and memory bounds for the C checker. Keel is correct-by-construction while also being faster than the BCF checker inside the kernel, 1.3X in total and 2.0X on the slowest 1.4% of certificates.

item.title: Statopia: A Prover–Library Ecosystem for Automated Formalization and Proof Discovery in Statistics
item.dc:creator: Ziyuan Chen, Tong Gan, Wei Zhang, Ruofei Fang, Boyue Tang, Zhenhua Lin, Fang Yao
item.description:
Builds an LLM-based agent that formalizes and proves statistics results in Lean 4, alongside Statlib, a Lean 4 statistics library on top of Mathlib.
Theoretical results in statistics and machine learning rest on long, technically delicate proofs, and fluent arguments generated by large language models are not necessarily correct. Automated formalization makes such arguments mechanically checkable, and automated proving goes further by discovering machine-checked proofs for statements whose proofs are incomplete or missing altogether. Both require reconstructing assumptions from source materials, accessing specialized mathematical infrastructure and managing long proof developments. We present Statopia, an ecosystem that jointly develops Statopia Prover, an independent agent specialized for formalizing and proving results in statistics and machine learning, and Statlib, a Lean 4 library built with the prover and organized for automated use. The prover controls its own execution without relying on external coding agents. It is built for formal proof discovery and checking existing proofs. A natural-language proof, when available, guides its search but is not required: from a statement alone, the prover develops the argument itself and constructs a Lean proof. Its workflow integrates source preparation, statement review, library supported planning and proof construction. Dynamic proof dependency graphs and task groups support parallel, resumable proof development. Statlib's shared definitions and theorem interfaces are organized for retrieval and composition by agents, and its coverage of statistics keeps expanding. Verified results and usage feedback from the prover inform reviewed library updates, so that proof development drives this expansion. A cross-platform application provides an interactive workspace for uploading source files and running tasks locally or in the cloud.

item.title: Bridging Gaps with Tensor Networks: From the Haldane Gap and Beyond
item.dc:creator: Sirui Lu
item.description:
Formalizes a reflection-positive spectral gap theorem for spin chains in Lean 4, with the Lean kernel checking the mixed-field Ising gap arithmetic unconditionally.
Proofs generated by large language models are often difficult to understand, generalize, or formalize directly. Here we verify, digest, and formalize OpenAI's computer-assisted proof of a uniform gap in the periodic spin-1 Heisenberg chain using tensor-network diagrams and Lean 4. Reading the partition-function network along space and imaginary time shows how finite-ring bounds propagate across doubled lengths and inverse temperatures to all longer even rings, sharpening the spin-1 bound from the same finite inputs by a factor of 19 to $Δ_L > 0.0729$ for all even $L \geq 36$. We identify reflection positivity as the general condition behind the proof and certify uniform gaps in seven additional spin chains and ladders. More broadly, digesting machine-generated proofs into transparent physical mechanisms yields sharper bounds, broader theorems, and reusable formal verifications.

item.title: The Herzog–Schönheim Conjecture for Solvable Groups
item.dc:creator: Murali Menon
item.description:
The full proof of the Herzog–Schönheim conjecture for solvable groups is formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with a public repository and axiom check.
The Herzog–Schönheim conjecture states that if a group is partitioned into finitely many, and at least two, cosets of subgroups, then two of these subgroups have the same index. We prove the conjecture for all solvable groups, finite or infinite. Sun's bound on unions of cosets, applied in a quotient, is combined with divisibility restrictions on local indices relative to the subgroup generated by the $p$-elements, where $p$ is the largest prime divisor of the order of a minimal counterexample. These restrictions are obtained by counting fixed points in a primitive solvable quotient. This suffices except at the prime $7$, where the counting bound narrowly fails and an additional overlap argument is needed. The proof has been formalized in Lean 4 with mathlib.

item.title: Improving Analytic Constants via Interpretable AI-Guided Lean Proof Refinement
item.dc:creator: Rahul Saha, Alan Li, Anton Xue, Swarat Chaudhuri, Adam Klivans, Pravesh K. Kothari, Raghu Meka
item.description:
An AI agent iteratively refines Lean code inside partially formalized Lean blueprints, with Lean checking the proof obligations alongside certified interval-arithmetic numerics, to tighten analytic constant bounds.
AI agents are increasingly capable of discovering new mathematical results, yet their reasoning and generated proofs can be difficult to understand and verify. We introduce an interpretable framework for AI-guided mathematical discovery, focused on improving quantitative bounds on analytic constants. Our key insight is that existing proofs often contain slack in intermediate lemmas, which can be tightened without reconstructing the entire argument. To exploit this structure, we represent proofs as partially-formalized Lean blueprints: human-interpretable dependency graphs of definitions, lemmas, and theorems. An AI agent then iteratively refines the Lean code while preserving the blueprint's dependency structure, allowing local improvements to automatically propagate to a verified final bound. This interpretable structure allows humans to inspect the agent's refinements and understand how local improvements propagate to the final theorem. For Grothendieck's constant ($\mathcal{K}_G$), we obtain $$ \mathcal{K}_G \leq \fracπ{2\log(1+\sqrt{2})} - 10^{-17}, $$ an explicit numerical improvement over Krivine's 1977 bound. For Korenblum's constant ($\mathcal{K}_K$), we obtain $$ \mathcal{K}_K \geq 0.356565, $$ improving Wang's 2025 bound of $0.3554$. Our experiments demonstrate the potential of both partial formalization and iterative agentic refinement for interpretable mathematical discovery.

item.title: Factor Rank: A Canonical Algebraic Generalization of Tree Decision Diagrams
item.dc:creator: Alexis de Colnet, Stefan Szeider
item.description:
Core theorems on ATDD canonicity, cut-space nesting, and vtree rotation are formalized and kernel-checked in Lean 4, with sources on Zenodo.
Tree decision diagrams (TDDs), recently introduced by Capelli et al. (SAT 2026), are representations of Boolean functions. They generalize OBDDs by replacing variable orders with vtrees. The width of a TDD counts the distinct subfunctions across each vtree cut. Counting subfunctions is blind to linear structure. We introduce algebraic tree decision diagrams (ATDDs) by replacing this count with the rank of the cut matrix. The maximum of these ranks over all cuts, the factor rank, is exactly the width of the ATDD. Every TDD can be converted into an ATDD of no greater width. An ATDD is a tree tensor network in canonical form. ATDDs are exponentially more succinct than TDDs, and quasi-polynomially more succinct than structured deterministic DNNFs. Our main result is that this gain in succinctness does not cost canonicity. ATDDs are the first strict canonical form for a rank-based representation over arbitrary vtrees. For each function and vtree there is exactly one ATDD, over the rationals and without any genericity assumption. The canonicity admits a local characterization. Whether a tree tensor network is the ATDD of the Boolean function it computes can be checked in polynomial time from its tensors alone. Equivalence checking becomes a test of syntactic equality. The operation set includes polynomial-time model counting, weighted model counting, and a test whether a tree tensor network represents a Boolean function. Capelli et al. asked for the complexity of changing the vtree of a TDD and suggested local vtree changes. We answer the question. After a rotation of the vtree at one node, the new ATDD differs from the old one in two tensors only. Vtree change runs in output-polynomial time both for TDDs and for ATDDs. We formalize and verify our core results in Lean. We provide a prototype implementation of TDD and ATDD compilers as a first empirical validation.

item.title: Extending DBLog-Based Incremental Snapshots to Handle Orphan Rows in CDC Pipelines
item.dc:creator: Andreas Andreakis
item.description:
Safety and convergence of the DBLog orphan-row deletion extensions are mechanically verified in Lean 4 alongside Isabelle/HOL, with published sources.
Applications use heterogeneous datastores where a source feeds sinks such as search indexes or data warehouses via change data capture (CDC). As transaction logs have limited retention, CDC alone cannot bootstrap sinks, and traditional approaches either stall source writes or hold back log events. DBLog-based incremental snapshots, adopted by Debezium and Flink CDC, read tables in chunks interleaved with the log without blocking writes or long log stalls and resume where they stopped. After the initial bootstrap, a sink can drift when losing change events or receiving unintended writes. Even a repeated bootstrap can leave orphan rows that exist in the sink and not at the source. A common remedy is to populate a new empty sink, but repairing an existing sink avoids parallel pipelines, a switch and serving traffic from a drifted sink until the new sink is ready. In DBLog's original design, each chunk only emits the latest state of the rows the table still contains, so it does not handle orphan rows. We extend DBLog to delete them using what a chunk read already knows, namely the keys that the range select did not return, emitting a new kind of event that sinks apply as deletes. We also add a repair request that an external process calls with orphan candidates, which the connector checks with its own read, emitting these events for keys confirmed absent. This enables three modes. In the fully integrated mode, every chunk pass removes the orphans it finds during full or periodic repairs. In the second mode, an external drift process hands suspected orphans to the connector. The third mode combines both and is what we recommend. Together, they turn DBLog into a complete data synchronization engine whether a sink catches up on live changes or missing rows, holds wrong column values, or contains orphan rows. Their safety and convergence are formally verified in Isabelle/HOL and Lean 4.

item.title: Formal Proof of an Anisotropic Calderón Uniqueness Theorem
item.dc:creator: Cătălin I. Cârstea, Lauri Oksanen
item.description:
Formalizes in Lean 4, using Mathlib and Tau Ceti, a special case of the anisotropic Calderón uniqueness theorem, checked via a comparator challenge.
We announce a Lean 4 formal proof of a special case of the smooth anisotropic Calderón uniqueness theorem released by OpenAI on October 6, 2026. We consider smooth Riemannian metrics on the three-dimensional unit ball, with full boundary measurements and Euclidean extensions outside the ball. OpenAI's release did not include a Lean proof of their uniqueness result. Our formalization uses results from Mathlib and Tau Ceti, and it is given as a solution to a Lean comparator challenge whose check permits only the standard axioms of Lean. The Lean proof is not a line-by-line translation of the OpenAI manuscript.

item.title: A trace costs one quantifier: the exact complexity of perfect play in nonlocal games
item.dc:creator: Seth Douglas, Nidhal Mghirbi
item.description:
Main theorem (Σ⁰₂-completeness of perfect spatial play, with and without finite entropy) is proved in Lean 4 with Mathlib, axiom-free beyond standard axioms, and kernel-checked independently.
Given a finite nonlocal game, can the players win with certainty? We prove that the existence of a perfect normal spatial strategy is $Σ^0_2$-complete, even when restricted to games of value one, so it cannot be decided even with an oracle for the halting problem. This is strictly harder than perfect play in the finite-dimensional and commuting-operator models, which are $Σ^0_1$-complete and $Π^0_1$-complete. Within the commuting model, the existence of a perfect normal strategy with a finite or semifinite von Neumann host is $Σ^0_2$-complete, whereas for every fixed type $\mathrm{III}_λ$ subtype it has the same $Π^0_1$-complete language as unrestricted commuting play. A trace thus costs one existential number quantifier: the hardness constructions force every perfect strategy to choose a finite clock period or a finite tree depth. Spatial $Σ^0_2$-completeness also holds when finite entanglement entropy is required, and both forms are formally verified in Lean. For every computable $0<α<1$, perfect spatial play with $\mathrm{Tr}\,h^α<\infty$ for the reduced density $h$ is $Σ^0_2$-complete as well; these conditions form a strict ladder between finite rank and finite entropy. We also prove $Σ^0_2$-completeness for one-shot zero-error communication with normal entanglement, and construct a finite channel with zero-error codes of a given size each of which needs infinite entanglement entropy.

item.title: A stability order barrier and SSP bound for Runge–Kutta methods with non-negative coefficients: AI-assisted proofs
item.dc:creator: Sigal Gottlieb, Zachary Grant, Lior Horesh, Lajos Lóczi, Avraham Shinnar, Barry Trager
item.description:
The paper's SSP bounds, phase-type moment inequalities and algebraic-stability order barrier are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with no sorry and only standard axioms.
We prove three results about Runge–Kutta methods with non-negative coefficients. First, every $s$-stage implicit Runge–Kutta method of order at least two has SSP coefficient at most $2s$; the bound is sharp and is attained by a known diagonally implicit method, so full implicitness gives no advantage over DIRK at second order. This extends the second-order DIRK result of Kocsis & Németh to full coefficient matrices and settles a conjecture of Ketcheson, Macdonald & Gottlieb. These proofs were found with the assistance of AI tools, which uncovered an interesting relationship between the Butcher matrices for SSP methods and phase-type distributions, and led to the proof of the second result: a bound on the SSP coefficient of $s$-stage implicit Runge–Kutta method of order at least three. The third result in this work is a proof that a third-order Runge–Kutta method with entrywise non-negative $A$ and $b$ cannot be algebraically stable. This algebraically intensive proof was also AI-assisted. This paper describes the iterative process of AI-assisted results, and presents an approach that centers human understanding and creativity in the AI-assisted mathematical endeavor.

item.title: Randomly shifted lattice rules for SDEs with constant diffusion: error bounds uniform in time discretization and dimension
item.dc:creator: Du Ouyang, Josef Dick, Ziyang Ye
item.description:
The main sampling-error theorems and corollary (Theorems 3.1, 3.6, 3.7, Corollary 3.3) are formalized in Lean 4, with a public repository.
We study randomly shifted rank-1 lattice rules for computing $\mathbb{E}[g(\mathbf{X}_T)]$, where $\mathbf{X}_T$ is the terminal state of a stochastic differential equation (SDE) with constant diffusion matrix. Discretizing the SDE by the Euler–Maruyama scheme with $m$ uniform time steps turns the expectation into an integral whose dimension grows with $m$ and whose integrand has a nested composition structure; both complicate the lattice rule error analysis. We generate the Brownian path by the Brownian bridge construction and handle the nested structure using the multivariate Faà di Bruno formula and a rooted-tree expansion. Under suitable regularity and growth conditions, we prove that an $N$-point randomly shifted lattice rule with a uniformly random generating vector achieves a mean absolute sampling error of $O(N^{-1+\varepsilon})$ for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$ and every prime $N$, with the implied constant independent of $m$. To improve stability and control higher error moments, the median lattice estimator is used. The estimator takes the median of $R=2k-1$ independent lattice estimates and achieves an $L^q$ error of $O(N^{-1+\varepsilon})$ for every $1\le q<k/(1-\varepsilon)$. We further establish error bounds independent of both the state dimension and the Brownian path dimension under an additional summability condition on the columns of the diffusion matrix. Numerical experiments show that median lattice estimators converge faster than Monte Carlo estimators and remain stable as the number of time steps $m$ grows. For models satisfying the additional summability condition, stability is also observed as the state and Brownian path dimensions increase.

item.title: Mahler's Problem on Liouville Numbers II. Rational Maps
item.dc:creator: Diego Marques
item.description:
The main equivalence (Theorem 1.2), characterizing which real rational functions map Liouville numbers into rationals or Liouville numbers, is formalized in Lean 4 in a public repository.
In 1984, Mahler asked which analytic functions map the set $\mathscr L$ of Liouville numbers into itself. In the first paper of this series, we proved that every real-analytic solution on an open interval is the restriction of a real rational function. We now identify a canonical subfield $\mathbb L$ of $\mathbb R$ such that, for every nonconstant $R\in\mathbb R(X)$ and every nonempty open interval $I$ in its domain, $R(I\cap\mathscr L)\subseteq\mathscr L$ if and only if $R$ is defined over $\mathbb L$ and $R^{-1}(\mathbb Q)\cap I\cap\mathscr L=\varnothing$. The weaker inclusion $R(I\cap\mathscr L)\subseteq\mathbb Q\cup\mathscr L$ holds if and only if $R$ is defined over $\mathbb L$. If $R$ is not defined over $\mathbb L$, every such interval contains a Cantor set of Liouville numbers whose images under $R$ are irrational and have irrationality exponents bounded by a constant depending only on $R$. We also construct continuum many positive strong Liouville numbers $σ$ for which $σX^m$ preserves $\mathscr L$ for every $m\geq2$, with all nonzero rational fibers consisting of $U_m$-numbers.

item.title: Compatible Hamel Topologies, Real Valued Isomorphisms and Rational Scalar Continuity
item.dc:creator: Irina Yaroshevskaya
item.description:
Selected results (chain criteria, two-chain counterexample, isomorphism classification, sequence and dimension results) were formalized and typechecked in Lean 4 with Mathlib in a public repository.
We study Hamel character topologies on the real line in two parts. Part I treats the full real-orbit (TVG) and the rational-parameter (TVGQ) dual pairs. A divisibility-chain criterion decides compatibility on the rationals and on Q/Z. Compatible subsets of one chain have a compatible join, but two different chains need not: an explicit Chinese remainder construction gives two compatible topologies with an incompatible join. This answers the compact-union question negatively, disproves the Greatest Compatible TVG Conjecture for every nonzero rational-valued Hamel functional, and shows that the corresponding rational and real dual pairs admit no Mackey topology. We classify additive homomorphisms and isomorphisms of the real-valued observation spaces and their automorphism groups, prove that both prime square-denominator topologies are non-nuclear, classify sequences converging for every coefficient functional, and show that the real parameters of continuous characters of the integers with the mixed-prime metric form a set of Hausdorff dimension zero. Part II studies real vector spaces whose Hausdorff additive group topology makes every fixed rational scalar multiplication continuous (TVGQ). A rational-valued Hamel functional and a rational parameter space S generate precompact, modular and real-valued observation topologies whose exact scalar ring is the multiplier ring of S. We compute their completions and character groups, classify the precompact TVGQ topologies, characterize universal separating sequences, show that local compactness and sigma-compactness force the scalar ring to be a field, classify isomorphisms within each modular family (exactly 2^c types), identify greatest-compatible existence with the unrestricted Mackey problem, and prove that all compatible topologies for the rational Hamel pair are non-Baire.

item.title: A family of symmetric counterexamples to the bent sum decomposition conjecture
item.dc:creator: Máté Róbert Kepes, Anita Kercsó-Molnár, András Viczián
item.description:
The main theorem and the bentness of an explicit eight-variable function are formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with an accompanying repository.
In this paper, we provide an infinite family of counterexamples to Tokareva's conjecture on sums of two bent functions. The conjecture states that every Boolean function in an even number of variables $n$ of algebraic degree at most $n/2$ can be written as the sum of two bent functions. We show that for every $n=2^k\geq 8$, the symmetric function $F_n=1+σ_2+σ_4+σ_6+\cdots+σ_{n/2}$ has degree $n/2$ and cannot be written as a sum of at most two bent functions. Here $σ_j$ is the elementary symmetric Boolean polynomial of degree $j$. Furthermore, we show that the eight-variable member of this family can be represented as the sum of exactly three bent functions. Using the connection between bent-sum decompositions and derivatives of bent functions, we also obtain an infinite family of balanced Boolean functions that cannot be derivatives of bent functions.

item.title: Nonisomorphic separable Banach spaces at Lipschitz distance one
item.dc:creator: Ryotaro Tanaka
item.description:
The main theorem, existence of nonisomorphic separable Banach spaces at Lipschitz distance one, is formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, partly adapting OpenAI's Lean code.
We construct nonisomorphic separable real Banach spaces whose multiplicative Lipschitz distance is one. Building on OpenAI's graph-space construction, we arrange two sequences of graph spaces into countably many blocks and form two spaces that differ by a single additional block. This block distinguishes their linear structures: one space contains a complemented copy of $\ell_1(c_0(\ell_2))$, whereas the other does not. By mapping the additional block to increasingly late positions and rearranging the remaining blocks, we obtain homeomorphisms whose Lipschitz constants and those of their inverses tend to one, while both spaces and their norms remain unchanged.

item.title: PCF All The Way Down
item.dc:creator: Taylor Dupuy, Alon Levy, Thomas Tucker, Zhuoran Wang
item.description:
The main theorem and a corollary on post-critically finite maps are formalized in Lean 4 against Mathlib, with a public repository and blueprint.
We prove that a finite surjective post-critically finite self-map of a variety in characteristic zero remains post-critically finite on every preperiodic integral effective divisor after passing to its periodic image with its return map. Iterating this result proves PCF all the way down. A detailed report on AI usage is contained in the manuscript.

item.title: Learning Coarse Spaces for Two-Grid Methods from Smoothed Errors with Applications to High-Contrast Porous Media Flow
item.dc:creator: Chenglong Bao, Chen Cui, Ruohua Li
item.description:
Lean 4 formal verification files accompany the work, apparently for the theoretical analysis, and are announced for release in the project repository.
Efficient two-grid solvers for high-contrast parametric elliptic problems require coarse spaces that capture error components poorly reduced by local smoothing. As these components vary with the problem parameters, repeatedly constructing parameter-adaptive coarse spaces can be computationally expensive. We propose a coarse-space learning method based on finite-step errors generated by additive Schwarz smoothing. For each training parameter, proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) of smoothed-error snapshots in the discrete energy inner product defines a reference coarse space. A continuous-coordinate neural generator is then trained using a basis-invariant, whitened subspace loss, enabling the prediction of parameter-adaptive coarse spaces on unseen grids. We establish discrete perturbation estimates relating coarse-space discrepancies to the associated nonsymmetric two-grid operators and derive conditional finite-step Krylov residual-polynomial bounds without assuming stationary energy contraction. Numerical experiments on high-contrast interface problems, moving-interface Darcy flow, and nonlinear Forchheimer flow demonstrate effective solver performance across varying parameters and grid resolutions. On the finest static test grid, with approximately 264 times as many degrees of freedom as the training grid, the learned spaces achieve FGMRES iteration counts close to those of parameter-specific POD references and comparable to GenEO spaces, while substantially reducing repeated coarse-space construction costs.

item.title: Structural Lower Bounds for Quantum Property Estimation with Persistent Memory
item.dc:creator: Ye Tao, Hong Shen
item.description:
Lean 4 was used, with AI assistance, to verify an earlier formalization of the complete-Pauli lower bound; no Lean artifact is cited.
In quantum property estimation, an experimenter estimates $\operatorname{Tr}(Oρ)$ for a family of observables from independent copies of an unknown state $ρ$ simultaneously to additive error $ε$. While quantum memory can dramatically reduce sample complexity, understanding the power of a modest register that remains coherent throughout an adaptive experiment has remained an open challenge because existing frameworks require optimizing over the infinite space of measurement trees. We overcome this barrier by developing a backward-induction framework based on operator resolvents. Rather than tracking path-dependent memory states across rounds, resolvent regularization cancels internal memory trajectories exactly, reducing the lower bound to an algebraic certificate computed directly from the target observables with sharp $Ω(1/ε^2)$ scaling. Our structural rule charges only the retained dimension $K$ under arbitrary adaptive instruments and unrestricted memory lifetime. Via symmetry reductions, it yields polynomial-size linear programs that establish the optimal linear $Ω(D/(Kε^2))$ trade-off for the $D^2-1$ Paulis, eliminating the cubic loss in prior bounds. For growing weight-$w$ Pauli strings ($w=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$) and quadratic Majorana cross-correlations, it proves lower bounds of $Ω(3^w/ε^2)$ and $Ω(n^2/(ε^2(1+\ln n)^2))$ against an indefinitely persistent memory of dimension $K=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$. These bounds match memoryless or commuting estimators within polylogarithmic factors, demonstrating that rank constraints on the persistent register fundamentally throttle observable overlap and prevent a modest coherent memory from overcoming the sample complexity barrier.

item.title: Low moments of sums of extended Rademacher random multiplicative functions
item.dc:creator: Christopher Atherfold, Maxim Gerspach, Jad Hamdan
item.description:
All results were formalised in Lean 4, with Claude generating the proofs, using Mathlib and the PNT+ project; axiom checks confirm nothing is left unproved.
Let $X^e \colon \mathbb{N} \to \{\pm 1\}$ be the random, completely multiplicative function whose values at the primes $(X^e(p))_{p \text{ prime}}$ are independent and uniformly distributed on $\{ \pm 1 \}$. Let $X=X^eμ^2$. We determine the order of magnitude of \[ \mathbb{E} \Bigg[ \bigg| \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\sum_{n \le x} X^e(n) \bigg|^{2 q} \Bigg]\quad \text{ and }\quad \mathbb{E} \Bigg[ \bigg|\sum_{n \le x} \frac{X(n)}{\sqrt{n}} \bigg|^{2 q} \Bigg] \] for $q\in [0,1]$, showing that a transition from better-than-square-root cancellation to growth like a power of $\log x$ occurs when $q$ crosses $1/2$. In particular, the first absolute moments are of order $(\log\log x)^{3/4}$. The proof proceeds by comparing these sums to integrals of random Euler products, which are then studied by analogy with Gaussian multiplicative chaos integrals. The main difficulty lies in proving the lower bound at $q=1/2$, for which we also adapt arguments from the study of random walks.

item.title: Recognizing Label-Connected Graphs
item.dc:creator: Ralf Klasing, George B. Mertzios, Hendrik Molter, Nils Morawietz, Paul G. Spirakis
item.description:
The classical T-/M-witness characterization of temporally connectable (gossiping) multigraphs is formalized in Lean 4, with the formalization provided as an artifact.
In classical gossiping, each participant initially knows a distinct piece of information. Whenever two participants call each other, they exchange everything they know. We study Gossiping: given an undirected multigraph whose vertices represent participants and whose edges represent available calls, decide whether the calls can be ordered so that every participant learns all information, using each edge at most once. Equivalently, can one time label per edge make the graph temporally connected by strict temporal paths? This recognition problem is NP-complete; we study its parameterized complexity. After linear-time preprocessing, we give an exact $O(3^{n/3}n^3)$-time algorithm and a deterministic $2^{O(tw)}n$-time algorithm, where $n$ is the number of vertices and $tw$ is the treewidth of the underlying simple graph. We introduce a Tree Contraction Rule that extends the treewidth algorithm to single-exponential algorithms for parameters that may remain small on dense graphs, such as tree-independence number and clique-width, without requiring a decomposition as input. For the excess $δ=m-(2n-4)$ over the minimum number of calls, where $m$ is the number of edges, we give a randomized $2^{O(δ)}n^3$-time algorithm with one-sided error. Its main subroutine solves Rooted Independent Cycle: finding a cycle through four prescribed vertices whose edges are independent in a represented linear matroid. We solve this problem deterministically in $2^{O(r)}m$ arithmetic operations over the finite field representing the matroid, where $r$ is its rank. Gossiping is polynomial-time solvable at maximum degree four, counting parallel edges, but NP-complete on planar simple graphs of maximum degree five. The treewidth algorithm yields a $2^{O(\sqrt n)}$-time algorithm on planar graphs.

item.title: Whose Effect Is It? How Objectives Inflate Learned Subspace Interventions
item.dc:creator: Toygar Tanyel, Serkan Ayvaz
item.description:
The paper's first-order theoretical results on activation-patching effects are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with sources released on GitHub.
Interpretability often locates concepts by copying part of a language model's state from one input into another (activation patching). A larger output change counts as stronger evidence that this part carries the concept. Methods that learn which part to copy often change the output more than the whole state does. By that reading, learned parts isolate the concept more cleanly. Yet the whole contains the part. So whose effect is this excess, the network's or the method's? Copying the whole state learns nothing, so it shows what the network produces. We prove that, to first order, the effects of orthogonal parts add up to that of the whole. A part therefore exceeds the whole exactly when the rest moves the output back, which does not require isolating the concept more cleanly. Objectives that reward a larger effect select such parts. Distributed alignment search with cross-entropy, for example, exceeds the whole-state copy just before the output on almost all tasks, and inside the network at most sites. In both, changing only its objective to target what the network produces removes most of the excess. It therefore comes largely from the objective, so a larger learned effect alone is not stronger evidence.

item.title: Distributed LTL Synthesis under Arbitrary Message Adversaries
item.dc:creator: Benedikt Bollig, Patricia Bouyer-Decitre, Matthias Függer, Dhrubajyoti Ghosh, Thomas Nowak, Nathalie Sznajder
item.description:
Main results are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, including new automata libraries, MSO formalization, and undecidability reductions to Mathlib's halting theorem.
Reactive synthesis is the problem of generating a program that produces outputs satisfying a logical specification for every input stream. We study distributed synthesis for two processes communicating in rounds over unreliable links, with at least one message delivered in every round. Despite this delivery guarantee, we show that synthesis from linear temporal logic specifications is undecidable, even when messages carry the processes' complete causal histories. More generally, we give a complete characterization of the communication restrictions that make synthesis decidable. Restrictions are described by a message adversary $A$, a set of allowed infinite graph histories: sequences of communication graphs, each specifying which messages are delivered in a round. Iterated chromatic subdivision associates these histories with points in the unit interval, yielding an image $π(A) \subseteq [0,1]$. For every $ω$-regular message adversary $A$, synthesis is decidable if and only if $π(A)$ is nowhere dense. In the decidable cases, our procedure takes a deterministic parity automaton for $A$ and a specification, decides realizability, and constructs a realizing distributed algorithm whenever one exists. Further, our topological arguments shed new light on the fundamental requirements of synthesis. They show that, for $ω$-regular message adversaries, synthesis is decidable if and only if consensus is repeatedly solvable in bounded time. This links two previously unrelated problems from formal verification and distributed computing through the processes' uncertainty about communication.

item.title: The Structure of a Non-Isometric Non-Contractive Bijection of a Hereditarily Precompact Quasi-Metric Space
item.dc:creator: Thomas Duzer
item.description:
The structure theorems and three spiral examples on quasi-metric dynamics are machine-checked in Lean 4 over Mathlib, with files archived on Zenodo.
On a hereditarily precompact quasi-metric space, every non-contractive bijection $F$ is asymptotically an isometry along its backward orbits: for all $a$ and $\varepsilon>0$, $0\le d(Fx,Fy)-d(x,y)<\varepsilon$ for $x$ far in the past of $a$ and all $y$. Zavarzina asked whether every such bijection of a precompact space is an isometry; the author's toll spiral (arXiv:2610.13973) answered no. Each such $F$ has a register, a quasi-pseudo-metric $λ^-\le d$ for which $F$ is an isometry, with round-trip distances totally bounded on orbits; after completion, $F$ acts on each orbit as a rotation of a compact monothetic group, its rigid shadow. The defect $d-λ^-$ from $x$ to $y$ is at most the fee of $x$ (the supremum of its defects to earlier iterates) and at least the excess of $x$'s fee over $y$'s now or at any earlier time, less their round-trip register distance; the fee never decreases forward along orbits and tends to zero backward. In this sense, every such $F$ is a toll over its rigid shadow. The fees bound the defect but do not determine it: three spirals show it can depend on $y$, vanish at a distant $y$ even when $x$ has a positive fee, and be positive toward later iterates of $x$. The toll-spiral paper asked whether every such map is conjugate to a tolled extension, a fixed toll zone over an isometric shadow, possibly with infinitely many zones. If only descents are charged, the answer is no, even up to bi-Lipschitz conjugacy; on each infinite orbit, a map is such an extension over its register exactly when its ascents carry no defect. Fees may vanish at any rate, but for zone tolls (two-valued, shift-monotone, subadditive along their routes) they reach zero at a finite depth. The general results hold on quasi-pseudo-metric spaces where every sequence has a left K-Cauchy subsequence; all but the statements listed at the end are machine-checked in Lean.

item.title: Finding and Certifying Weighted Minimum Cuts with Cut Queries
item.dc:creator: Troy Lee
item.description:
Develops a Lean 4 library for cut-query algorithms that formalizes the paper's certificate and deterministic minimum-cut results, with an appendix mapping theorems to Lean statements.
We study the deterministic and nondeterministic cut query complexity of minimum cut in undirected graphs with arbitrary nonnegative edge weights. For the nondeterministic case, we show that every $n$-vertex graph has an $O(n\log^2(2n))$-query certificate of its exact global minimum-cut value, such that any other nonnegatively weighted graph on the same vertex set that agrees on these queries has the same minimum cut value. A key ingredient is a way to certify a maximum $s$–$t$ flow value with only $O(n)$ cut queries. For the deterministic case we give an algorithm that finds an exact global minimum cut using $O(n^{3/2}\log^3(2n)(\log\log(2n))^2)$ cut queries. Previously no $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ deterministic bound was known for arbitrary nonnegatively weighted graphs. The algorithm follows Karger's two-respecting tree approach. The key new ingredient is a deterministic construction of a weak skeleton of the input graph $G$: an explicit weighted graph $H$ in which every minimum cut of $G$ is a $5/4$-approximate minimum cut.

item.title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
item.dc:creator: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg, Katerina Hristova, George Tsoukalas, Johannes Bausch, Eric Wieser, Francisco J. H. Heras, Nicholas C. Rubin, Guang Hao Low, Sébastien Racanière, Nenad Tomašev, Lei M. Zhang, James Watson, Tanuj Khattar, Aws Albarghouthi, Stavan Jain, Harun Khan, Leopoldo Sarra, Andrew W. Senior, Michael Broughton, Hussain Masoom, Sergio Boixo, Ryan Babbush, Swarat Chaudhuri, Pushmeet Kohli
item.description:
Builds a Lean library of quantum programs where LLM agents synthesize programs against formal specifications and prove their correctness and cost.
The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which large language model agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 1.4x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

item.title: Braid Groups in Lean : Formalizing Dehornoy's Subword Reversing Algorithm
item.dc:creator: Hannah Fechtner
item.description:
Formalizes Artin braid groups in Lean and implements Dehornoy's subword reversing algorithm, proving its termination and correctness, building on Mathlib's Coxeter groups and Ore localization.
We formalize the group-theoretic definition of infinite and finite Artin braid groups in Lean. We implement a polynomial-time procedure for determining equivalence in the braid group known as Dehornoy's subword reversing algorithm. Termination and correctness of this algorithm are shown using rectangular grids, which are a specific form of van Kampen diagram. The literature only hints at a proof linking rectangular grids to braid equivalence. We present a novel, three-stage proof of this result, introducing partial grids and associated size metrics.

item.title: The Localization Scale of the Block Anderson Model in One Dimension at Arbitrary Coupling and Volume
item.dc:creator: Jun Yin
item.description:
The main localization-length theorem (Theorem 1.4) is formalized in Lean using only Mathlib, with proofs written with AI assistance; a public repository is provided.
We study the one-dimensional block Anderson model with independent $W\times W$ Gaussian unitary ensemble potentials and deterministic nearest-neighbor hopping, with hopping-to-disorder ratio $g$. The system consists of $L$ blocks, with total dimension $N=WL$. As $W\to\infty$, we identify the bulk localization length, up to an arbitrarily small power of $W$, with $\min\{N,\max\{W,W^2g^2\}\}$, uniformly for deterministic couplings $g\ge0$ and cycle lengths $L\ge3$. For every fixed $D>0$ and all sufficiently large $W$, the expected fraction of eigenvectors in the selected energy interval satisfying these bounds is at least $1-W^{-D}$. In polynomial volume the bounds hold simultaneously for all eigenvectors in that interval with probability at least $1-W^{-D}$. The localization length is the number of coordinates in the shortest cyclic interval containing at least half of an eigenvector's mass.

item.title: A proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture
item.dc:creator: David Turturean
item.description:
The main theorem and its corollary for the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture are formalized and kernel-checked in Lean, with a public repository.
Aaronson and Ambainis conjectured that every bounded polynomial of low degree on the discrete cube has an influential variable. They showed that the conjecture implies that the acceptance probability of every quantum algorithm making $T$ queries can be approximated on most inputs by a classical algorithm making $\mathrm{poly}(T)$ queries. We prove their conjecture: every function $f\colon\{-1,1\}^n\to[-1,1]$ of degree at most $d\ge1$ has a variable of influence at least $c\,\operatorname{Var}(f)^{5/2}/d^{6}$, where $c>0$ is an absolute constant. In the original formulation, for polynomials of degree at most $d$ with values in $[0,1]$ on $\{0,1\}^n$ and variance at least $\varepsilon$, this gives a variable of influence at least $(\varepsilon/d)^{7}$. The proof is elementary, with steps inspired by works of others. Thus, as Aaronson and Ambainis anticipated, superpolynomial quantum speedups in the query model require structure, such as a promise on the inputs.

item.title: Annular webs and Guralnick's conjecture
item.dc:creator: Tom Goertzen, Abel Lacabanne, Daniel Tubbenhauer, Pedro Vaz
item.description:
A Lean formalization verifies the explicit affine Weyl group family, the web calculation, gallery counts, and the row-sum identity for all m ≥ 2.
Using annular webs and Kazhdan-Lusztig mu-coefficients, we disprove Guralnick's absolute boundedness conjecture for first cohomology.

item.title: Resolvent-Diagonal Energy of Isospectral Jacobi Matrices
item.dc:creator: Dmitry Pasechnyuk-Vilensky, Martin Takáč
item.description:
The paper's mathematical results on resolvent-diagonal energy of isospectral Jacobi matrices are accompanied by formal proofs in Lean.
We study the minimum squared resolvent diagonal among Jacobi matrices with prescribed eigenvalues. For the zeros of $P_n^{(α,β)}$, we construct a canonical realization and bound its asymptotic cost against the optimum. Its rescaled inverse converges to the Green operator of a reflection-symmetric singular Schrödinger operator with Bessel-zero spectrum. A Green-coordinate identity places this construction and all finite realizations in the same density framework. Mass-constrained spectral problems then give computable lower bounds. The bounds meet at $α=1/2$, with optimal energy $2/15$, and have first-order contact with derivative $-13/75$. We classify the constrained extremal profiles and the three endpoint geometries of the canonical density. Two polynomial families with the same limiting edge spectrum have different limiting optimal energies. For Nesterov momentum $(s-1)/(s+1)$, the optimal leading endpoint Hessian-drift gain among nonnegative-link Jacobi realizations is $\sqrt{2}$ times the original gain. An explicit isospectral flow strictly improves the standard one-sided realization for $α>-1/2$, $α\ne1/2$.

item.title: LeanDojo-v2: A Comprehensive Library for AI-Assisted Theorem Proving in Lean
item.dc:creator: Ryan Hsiang, William Adkisson, Robert Joseph George, Anima Anandkumar
item.description:
Provides a Lean 4 library unifying repository data extraction, LLM fine-tuning, proof search, and tactic suggestion, plus a Lean-native VSCodium-based IDE.
Building on recent progress in machine learning for formal theorem proving in Lean, we introduce LeanDojo-v2: an end-to-end framework that unifies repository data extraction, LLM fine-tuning, proof search, AI autocompletion, and LLM-assisted theorem proving in a single software library. In addition, we provide Lean4Code, a lightweight IDE that integrates the various features of LeanDojo-v2 through a simple, mathematician-friendly UI. These tools will enable mathematicians and researchers to easily fine-tune language models on domain-specific Lean codebases and experiment with LLM-assisted theorem proving without a complex setup.

item.title: Joint Approximation and the Mixed-Prime Character Group
item.dc:creator: Irina Yaroshevskaya
item.description:
The joint approximation theorem and the one-prime character theorem are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, conditional on an unformalized two-term logarithmic separation hypothesis.
For the integer metric defined by the square denominators of two distinct primes, we prove simultaneous approximation to zero in one prime metric and to any prescribed integer in the other. A normalized convolution argument gives a uniform central spectral bound. Random relative translations of smooth weights produce an exact positive cas cade; Fourier positivity places every normalized finer convolution below its value at zero. A far-field recursion, the growth of merged square powers, and a two-term logarithmic-form estimate give summable fac tor bounds. Consequently, for every fixed pair of distinct primes p,q, the mixed continuous character group is Z[1/(pq)]/Z: no irrational pa rameter is continuous. The mixed completion is the product of the one-prime completions. For each fixed pair this also gives a compati ble rational join and a strictly finer compatible join of the associated real TVG topologies, with the same prescribed real character group. Exact witness search terminates at every strict precision and integer target. We retain the structural, density, divisibility, sequence and finite-certificate results leading to this proof. The existence argument does not give practical witness-size or runtime bounds, and it does not assume independence or equidistribution of the two digit systems. Se lected abstract components have been checked using Lean and Mathlib; the complete analytic argument has not been formalized. The corre sponding problem for three or more primes remains separate.

item.title: Lea: An Agent Backbone for Mathematician-Controlled Formalization in Lean
item.dc:creator: Shaswat Patel, Daniel Aarao Reis Arturi, Kevin Gomez, Jaume de Dios Pont, Jorge Poco, Eduardo V. Teixeira, Sam Westrick, Claudio Silva, Chinmay Hegde
item.description:
Builds an open-source Lean-specific agent backbone with LSP, Loogle, blueprints and SafeVerify, and uses it to formalize the Durfee square generating function from Mathlib.
Agentic systems now formalize research-level mathematics in Lean, but they are built for autonomy: the mathematician states a target and inspects a result. The alternative, a general-purpose coding harness, is domain-neutral and must be assembled into a formalization workspace before any mathematics begins. Mathematicians, however, report wanting to keep high-level control over how an argument is decomposed and established. We present $\textbf{Lea}$, a Lean-specific agent backbone for mathematician-facing software rather than a single interface. Lea exposes runs, sessions, and typed events through one application-neutral API, and ships with Lean tooling (blueprints, LSP, Loogle, SafeVerify) already wired. We report two applications built on it: $\textbf{LeaChat}$, a web client for interactive proof authoring, and $\textbf{LeaOverleaf}$, which formalizes theorems annotated directly in an Overleaf document; a session begun in either continues in the other. In a case study, a mathematician outlined a proof of the Durfee square generating function in a few natural-language messages, and Lea produced a complete Lean development from Mathlib alone, following the intended decomposition closely and requiring substantive correction at a single point. Lea and both applications are released as open source so that further mathematician-facing tools can be built on the same backbone.

item.title: Conley index theory for asymptotically autonomous systems and UV-to-IR connections
item.dc:creator: Alireza Behtash, Syo Kamata, Mauricio M. Martinez
item.description:
The paper's results on Conley index theory for asymptotically autonomous systems were formalized in Lean 4 with AI assistance; the formalization compiles without unproved steps and is publicly released.
Many non-equilibrium systems, such as expanding plasmas, evolve by equations that depend explicitly on time and interpolate between autonomous early-time (UV) and late-time (IR) limits. After time is compactified, fixed points lie on invariant boundary fibers, where the Conley index is one-sided and blind to the UV. For time dependence that admits a $C^1$ compactification, we reflect the extended phase space across these fibers. Both sheets of the double run from the UV to the IR, and the UV index reappears, suspended by one degree. Extending one sheet slightly beyond both fibers gives an explicit UV-to-IR transport map between the Conley indices of the limit systems, and its non-vanishing forces connecting solutions. If one block with a fixed strict entrance/exit decomposition serves every frozen system, this map is an isomorphism at every admissible rate. If the block also has nonzero relative homology, the isolated invariant sets of the two limits are connected at every rate. In the Gubser flow of Israel-Stewart theory, the separatrix between two classes of initial data is a transversal connection at every finite relaxation scale $c$, with splitting $Δ(c)\propto1/c$. In the Bjorken flow at the lowest moment truncation, we prove existence and uniqueness of the attractor solution without regularization. For the three-dimensional Gubser system we construct the global Morse decomposition. In the one-loop flow of the $(4+ε)$-dimensional $O(N)$ model with cubic anisotropy, a shift of $N$ through $N=4$ has vanishing transport map, but a driven connection and a nonzero connecting homomorphism detect it at every rate.

item.title: A uniform double-factorial construction for consecutive-pattern packings
item.dc:creator: Zoltán Nagy
item.description:
The main counting theorem, that the packings of the constructed pattern number (2j-1)!!, is formalized in Lean 4/Mathlib in an accompanying archive.
For every overlap $m\geq 3$ and every pattern length $K\geq 2m+1$, we construct an explicit permutation $p\in\mathfrak{S}_K$ such that the number of permutations containing $j$ prescribed occurrences of $p$, with successive starts separated by $K-m$, is $(2j-1)!!$ for every $j\geq 1$. Additional occurrences are permitted. We prove that the corresponding occurrence poset is the ordinal sum of a chain on $m+j(K-m-2)$ elements and a comb on $2j$ elements. An insertion bijection counts the linear extensions of the comb. This gives the uniform representatives requested in the double-factorial part of Question 6 in Section 7 of Blitvić, Kammoun and Steingrímsson, arXiv:2610.29846v1. A Lean 4 formalization and its recorded verification data accompany the paper.

item.title: The most entangled states of four and seven qubits
item.dc:creator: Antony Lewis
item.description:
Formalizes the four-qubit entropy maximum, its equality case, spectral corollaries, stability estimates and icosahedral-family computations in Lean 4 with Mathlib.
Pure states of four and seven qubits cannot be maximally entangled across every balanced bipartition; we determine how entangled they can be on average. For four qubits we prove the conjecture of Higuchi and Sudbery: the mean von Neumann entropy of the three $2|2$ cuts is at most $1+\tfrac12\log_2 3$ bits, with equality exactly on the local-unitary orbits of their state $M_4$ and its complex conjugate. For seven qubits the mean purity of the 35 balanced $3|4$ cuts is at least $121/917$ and their mean entropy is at most $2.965356029\ldots$ bits, each with a unique optimiser up to local unitaries and qubit permutations. The two optimisers are distinct members of one icosahedral family, so minimum purity and maximum entropy select different states. The proofs bound moments of the marginal spectra by positive identities on several copies of the state, some of them spin flipped, and bound the entropy by a polynomial in those moments. The four-qubit maximum has an analytic proof; the seven-qubit proofs, and some of the four-qubit refinements below, are computer-assisted, with exact arithmetic and rigorous error bounds. We also prove the Gour–Wallach conjecture for Rényi entropies of all orders, with the maximiser changing from $M_4$ to cluster states at $q_*\approx1.588$, and obtain sharp Tsallis bounds, mixed-state bounds and quantitative stability.

item.title: Equilateral sets in $\ell_p^n$ beyond $n+1$: Linear excess and dimension cost
item.dc:creator: Logan R. Chalmers, Aran S. Ziegler
item.description:
The equilateral-set constructions and finite bounds in ℓ_p^n are formalised in Lean, with the formalisation archived on Zenodo.
How many equilateral points can $\ell_p^n$ contain beyond $n+1$? For every fixed real $p>4$, we construct equilateral sets for which the number of points beyond $n+1$ grows at least linearly with $n$. For every fixed dimension, we prove that the maximum is $n+1$ at all sufficiently large finite $p$, with an explicit threshold. The least dimension admitting any fixed number of extra points is $p^{1+o(1)}$ as $p\to\infty$. The constructions and finite bounds are formalised in Lean. Thus $p=4$ marks the boundary: $n+1$ is exact in every dimension for $2\leq p\leq4$, while at every fixed finite $p>4$ the excess grows at least linearly with dimension.

item.title: ScienceCUA: Resource-to-Skill Construction and Execution-Guided Skill Evolution for Scientific Computer Use Agents
item.dc:creator: Daiqiang Li, Jingyi Peng, Rui Hu, Jia Li, Xuyang Liu, Guanren Qiao, Yujia Xiang, Qiuzhuang Sun, Zhiping Xu, Mingrui Luo
item.description:
Lean 4 (v4.14.0) is one of six scientific applications. Agents solve formal-proof tasks in it, and the authors audited and added Lean benchmark tasks.
Computer-use agents for scientific software require application-specific expertise. Much of this expertise is documented in human-authored software manuals and web pages. However, turning these resources into executable, reusable skills remains challenging due to mismatches between documented and deployed software versions and differences in scope between documentation coverage and task requirements. We introduce ScienceCUA, a two-stage framework combining resource-to-skill construction with execution-guided skill evolution. First, ScienceCUA identifies tasks supported by the software from its documentation, infers operational trajectories, and generalizes them into reusable Skills. Command catalogs, syntax constraints, and shortcuts are organized separately as References for on-demand lookup. Then, ScienceCUA uses execution feedback to drive skill self-evolution by contrasting successful and failed trajectories for the same task, identifying deficiencies, revising existing skills or adding new ones, and updating the skill library only after repeated validation in real environments. To enable reliable evaluation without benchmark noise or task leakage, we introduce two improved benchmarks. ScienceBoard-Verified provides an audited and corrected basis for measuring task performance, while ScienceBoard-VE separates skill evolution from final testing through disjoint evolution and test tasks and further supports native-agent evaluation. Experiments show that the initial Skills and References improve average task success rate by up to 7.23 percentage points over the base model, while skill self-evolution increases the total gain over the baseline to as much as 17.12 percentage points. ScienceCUA turns software documentation into an evolving set of executable skills and queryable references, offering a practical way for general-purpose agents to use scientific software reliably and at scale.

item.title: Old Is Not False: Valid-Time Memory for Interactive Video World Models
item.dc:creator: Ziming Wang, Chuyue Gong, Hongliang Cao, Jingmin Zhu, Chutian Wang, Yuheng He, Xiuyu Li
item.description:
The deterministic theoretical results about timestamp rules and valid-time memory are machine-checked in Lean 4 in a supplementary file, ReDate.lean.
Interactive video world models draw each frame from a memory bank of earlier frames stamped with their capture times. With frames, weights and noise fixed, reversing the timestamps of two views flips the state that generators of two families draw: they take the newest timestamp as the truth. That reading is right as long as states never return. After an agent undoes an action, the newest view of a region is outdated and the only view of the present is older; memories for changing worlds delete that older view, and memories that keep it hand the generator the past. Temporal databases separate when a record is stored from when its content holds, its valid time. ReDate keeps every frame and dates each retrieved token by its valid time, read from the agent's action log. The frozen generator then reads a reverted region as one that has just reached a new state, so ReDate needs no training. We prove that trusting the newest timestamp is right exactly when every current view is dated after every outdated one, that without a view taken after the return only the action log tells a reverted region from an up-to-date one, and that a generator able to draw from its own prediction gains more from re-dating than from deletion when the moved tokens keep little weight. After an undo, ReDate raises the share of FAR's steps showing the current state from 0.36 to 0.62 and HY-WorldPlay's from 0.003 to 0.19. We also propose a calibrated state metric to test any memory after undos.

item.title: Matrix Multiplication from Polynomial Packings: A Constructive and Elementary Proof of $ω\le9/4$
item.dc:creator: Rafael Pass
item.description:
Aristotle generated an approximately 3,600-line Lean 4 formalization of the matrix-multiplication identities and the operation bound, using Mathlib's matrix definitions.
We give a self-contained constructive proof that the matrix multiplication exponent satisfies $ω\le9/4$. In a recent breakthrough, OpenAI \cite{original} established this bound in the model of exact scalar arithmetic over the complex numbers, using non-constructive arguments in Strassen's asymptotic spectral framework. We explicitly construct a Strassen-style matrix multiplication identity and obtain the bound by ordinary block recursion. For every $γ>0$, the resulting algorithm multiplies two $n\times n$ integer matrices using $O(n^{9/4+γ})$ integer arithmetic operations. As an independent contribution, we develop a framework of polynomial packings—methods for reducing many polynomial multiplications to fewer ones using linear operations. We isolate and generalize a construction of OpenAI \cite{original} to obtain a simple packing, and show how packings can be composed to amplify their “compression rate", which finally yields Strassen-like identities.

item.title: What makes a theorem interesting? Operationalizing interestingness for open-ended exploration
item.dc:creator: Silvère Gangloff
item.description:
Uses Mathlib's hand-written theorems, with statement, proof and dependency features and curated 'main results' labels, as the main corpus for modeling theorem interestingness.
An agent that explores, whether it generates conjectures or research ideas, must decide which of them are worth keeping. This judgment of interestingness is usually delegated to a hand-picked proxy or to a language model, neither of which is known to correspond to what humans actually value. I study it for mathematical theorems, by observing which results mathematicians single out in formal libraries and in papers. I model each way of singling out results as an evaluator that weights features of a result's statement, its proof and dependencies, and split its weights into a shared and a subjective part. In formalized mathematics, ex-ante features predict these selections as well as a large language-model judge, and the two complement each other. Interestingness is also largely shared. One set of weights, carried mostly by structural features such as the length of the statement and of the proof and the subfields the proof draws on, accounts for most of the signal and transfers in part across formal libraries. What remains subjective depends on practices and individual authors more than on subfields. The judge's advantage lies in its knowledge of the canon, and neither the judge nor the features rely on memory of the papers. The approach, which infers what a community finds interesting from what it singles out, can be applied to other sciences.

item.title: On Lattice Tilings by Symmetric Limited Magnitude Error Balls: Q-polynomials and Ideal Characterization
item.dc:creator: Ang Xiao
item.description:
All statements except those relying on Maple computations are formalized and machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, using only standard axioms.
In this paper, we study the lattice tilings of $\mathbb{Z}^n$ by the symmetric limited magnitude error balls $\mathcal{B}(n,t,k,k)$, which play a crucial role in flash memory applications. Using generating functions and complete Bell polynomials, we derive an explicit formula for the $r$-th Q-polynomial associated with $\mathcal{B}(n,t,k,k)$. Then, an ideal-theoretic characterization of the lattice tiling condition is developed: for an odd prime $p$ dividing $|\mathcal{B}(n,t,k,k)|$ exactly once, a lattice tiling would force a certain polynomial to lie outside a certain ideal of $\mathbb{F}_p[Y_1,\dots,Y_{\frac{p-1}{2}}]$. Applying this criterion yields congruence conditions on the dimension $n$ that rule out lattice tilings; for $2\le t\le10$ and $1\le k\le10$, a systematic Maple computation over all primes $3\le p\le29$ excludes, on average, $35.65\%$ of all dimensions, with a maximum of $76.69\%$. Finally, we obtain two infinite families of parameters $(n,t,k)$ for which no lattice tiling exists: no lattice tiling exists if $k\equiv4\pmod9$ and the base-$3$ addition of $t$ and $n-1-t$ produces exactly one carry; and no lattice tiling of $\mathbb{Z}^n$ by $\mathcal{B}(n,n-1,k,k)$ exists if $k\equiv8\pmod9$ and $n\equiv2,4\pmod6$. Their sizes are also estimated.

item.title: Modern Software Engineering with Verification Agents: A Spec-First Architecture for Autonomous Synthesis, Verification IRs, and Organizational Scale
item.dc:creator: Jason Hickey
item.description:
Builds on the authors' Lean 4 artifacts (salt review gates, x86lean ISA semantics, vir IR) and contrasts idiomatic Lean specifications with extensional CTT.
When autonomous coding agents synthesize implementation code, formal specifications, and mechanical proofs simultaneously, the software engineering hierarchy inverts: the formal specification becomes the primary human-reviewed artifact, while source code and proof scripts become disposable build outputs. This paper presents an end-to-end architecture for agent-authored, formally verified software engineering. First, we establish a logic-agnostic foundation combining a spec-first stack inversion, a zero-code-review workflow gated by automated continuous integration (CI) checks, and a minimal Verification Intermediate Representation (VIR) lowered via a thin, verified translator. Second, we pair an extensional Computational Type Theory (CTT) specification layer with Higher-Order Abstract Syntax (HOAS) and linear resource typing in the VIR–eliminating rewrite friction for synthesis agents while defining an experiment, its protocol frozen before the first reader, to measure whether removing boundary coercions improves human specification readability. Third, we scale collaboration across multi-team organizations using Personal Spec-Copilots and a Shared Synthesis Fleet that detects cross-team Semantic Merge Conflicts and fuses modular contracts into zero-copy binaries. We illustrate this architecture on a zero-copy authenticated message router and distinguish our existing empirical baselines (salt, SaltBench, x86lean, and MetaPRL) from newly proposed components.

item.title: Computation in Anonymous Directed Dynamic Networks: Exact Worst-Case Termination Time and Network-Wise Intractability
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe A. Di Luna, Giovanni Viglietta
item.description:
